modules.title: Foundations
modules.blurb: What regression is, and the two jobs it does for managers.
concepts: What regression does

Regression measures how an outcome moves with the factors that drive it, and attaches a measure of uncertainty to every estimate. That second part is what turns a hunch into an analysis: a manager learns not only that revenue rises with deal size, but how much, and how sure we can be.
Explain or predict

Regression does two jobs. Explanation asks which factors move the outcome, holding the others constant; the coefficients are the product. Prediction asks what value to expect for a new case; accuracy on unseen data is the product. Decide which question you are answering before you build, because the evidence you need and the way you judge success are different.
Outcome and predictors

The outcome (Y) is what you want to explain or forecast: NovaTech's monthly revenue per deal, whether a Mercy Regional patient is readmitted within 30 days, or Riverside County's processing days. Predictors (X) are the drivers you believe matter. An outcome can be dollars, days, or a yes/no event.
The modeling process

Frame the decision, gather and clean the data, explore it with plots, fit the model, evaluate it on assumptions and unseen data, then communicate in dollars, days or patients with an honest range. Fitting takes seconds; framing, exploring and evaluating are where models succeed or fail.
cards: The outcome you want to explain or forecast. Also called the response.
A factor believed to drive the outcome. Also called a predictor or, in machine learning, a feature.
Estimating how much each driver moves the outcome, holding the others constant. The coefficients are the product.
Forecasting the outcome for new cases. Accuracy on data the model has not seen is the product.
Historical data → model → prediction → decision. The decision's outcome becomes new data, and the model is checked and refit.
Comparing cases that differ in one predictor while every other predictor in the model stays fixed.

kc.stem: The finance team needs next quarter's revenue figure for the budget. Which job is regression doing?
opts: Predicting a value for a new case
kc.why: The team needs a number for a case that hasn't happened yet. Accuracy on new data is what matters, so this is prediction.

kc.stem: Mercy Regional asks which patients are likely to be readmitted within 30 days. What is the outcome (Y)?
opts: Whether the patient is readmitted within 30 days
kc.why: The outcome is the thing being explained or forecast: readmission. The others are candidate predictors.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes regression?
opts: It proves which factors cause an outcome
It estimates how an outcome changes with one or more predictors, with a measure of uncertainty
It summarizes the spread of a single variable
quiz.why: Regression estimates relationships and their uncertainty. Whether a relationship is causal depends on how the data were generated.

quiz.stem: Riverside County models processing days from caseworker ratio and digital access. In this model, the caseworker ratio is:
quiz.why: Processing days is the outcome; caseworker ratio is one of the drivers, a predictor.

quiz.stem: Which step should come before fitting a model?
opts: Testing the model on held-out data
Plotting the outcome against each predictor
quiz.why: Explore first: plots reveal direction, shape and unusual points before any coefficients are estimated.

quiz.stem: Why does the predictive-modeling loop 'close'?
opts: Because a model is final once it is fit
Because the outcomes of decisions become new data used to check and refit the model
Because predictions replace the need for data
Because the intercept resets each cycle
quiz.why: A model never checked against what actually happened should not be trusted. Outcomes feed back into the next fit.

quiz.stem: A model will be judged by how close its forecasts come to next quarter's actual sales. Its primary job is:
quiz.why: When success is measured by accuracy on future cases, the job is prediction.

quiz.stem: A hospital models length of stay from patient age and ICU admission. Which is the outcome?
quiz.why: The outcome is what the model explains or forecasts; age and ICU admission are predictors.

quiz.stem: Which of these is an explanation question?
opts: Does weekend discharge raise readmission risk once patient complexity is accounted for?
What will revenue be next quarter?
How many leads will next month's campaign produce?
How many applications will arrive next week?
quiz.why: Explanation asks how much a driver moves the outcome, holding others constant. The others ask for a forecast.

quiz.stem: Which step of the modeling process turns coefficients into dollars, days or patients with an honest range?
quiz.why: Communicating translates results into managerial units with uncertainty, so a decision can follow.

checkpoint.stem: Which job is regression doing when the question is “what value should we expect for a new case?”
checkpoint.why: Forecasting a new case is prediction; accuracy on unseen data is what matters.

modules.title: Simple Linear Regression
modules.blurb: One predictor, one line, built from first principles.
concepts: The line

Simple regression summarizes a scatter plot with Y = b₀ + b₁X + ε. The intercept b₀ is the predicted Y when X is zero; the slope b₁ is the change in predicted Y for a one-unit increase in X; ε is everything the line misses. The gap between an actual value and the line's prediction is the residual.
Least squares

Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. Squaring stops positive and negative misses from cancelling and makes large misses count more. The slope is Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ Σ(x − x̄)², and the line always passes through the point of means.
Reading the NovaTech line

For 48 campaigns, Leads = 172.5 + 0.0155 × Spend. Campaigns that spent $1,000 more generated about 15.5 more leads, on average. The intercept anchors the line but is not a forecast for zero spend: no campaign spent under $2,849. Turned into a price, each additional lead costs about 1 ÷ 0.01546 ≈ $65, against a $38 average.
How much to trust it

R² = 0.63: spend accounts for about 63% of the variation in leads. The slope's standard error is 0.00176, t = 8.79, p < 0.0001, and the 95% confidence interval is 11.9 to 19.0 leads per $1,000. Plan with the range, not the single number.
Bends and causes

The biggest campaigns fall below the line. A log-log model gives an elasticity of 0.70: 10% more spend is associated with about 6.9% more leads, which is diminishing returns. And a slope is association: if budgets peak in high season, season drives both spend and leads, and part of the slope belongs to the season.
cards: Actual value minus predicted value: e = Y − Ŷ. The vertical miss between a point and the line.
Chooses b₀ and b₁ to make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible.
Change in predicted Y for a one-unit increase in X. NovaTech: about 15.5 leads per $1,000.
Predicted Y when X = 0. Often outside the data; it anchors the line rather than forecasting.
Share of the outcome's variation the model explains: SSR ÷ SST. Describes fit, not cause.
The range of plausible values for a coefficient. Slope: 11.9 to 19.0 leads per $1,000.
Slope in a log-log model: the % change in Y for a 1% change in X. 0.70 means diminishing returns.
A factor that drives both X and Y, so part of the slope belongs to it. Example: season drives budgets and leads.

kc.stem: With a slope of 0.0155 leads per dollar, how many more leads would you expect from $2,000 more spend?
R² = 0.63 in the NovaTech marketing model means:
opts: About 63% of the variation in leads is accounted for by spend
63% of campaigns sit on the line
kc.why: R² is the share of variation explained by the model. It says nothing about cause or coefficient accuracy.

quiz.stem: Ordinary least squares chooses the line that minimizes:
opts: The number of points off the line
quiz.why: Squared residuals can't cancel, and large misses count more.

quiz.stem: The 95% CI for the slope is 11.9 to 19.0 leads per $1,000. The best conclusion is:
opts: The effect is plausibly between about 12 and 19 leads per $1,000, and clearly above zero
95% of campaigns fall in that range
quiz.why: The interval gives plausible values for the average effect. Zero is far outside it.

quiz.stem: If one dollar buys 0.01546 leads, the cost of one additional lead is about:
quiz.why: 1 ÷ 0.01546 ≈ $65 per additional lead, compared with a $38 average.

quiz.stem: In a log-log model the slope is 0.70. A 10% increase in spend is associated with:
quiz.why: The slope is an elasticity: 1.10^0.70 ≈ 1.069, about 6.9% more leads.

quiz.stem: NovaTech sets its largest budgets in peak season. Why does this threaten a causal reading of the slope?
opts: Season may drive both spend and leads
The intercept is outside the data
quiz.why: A confounder that moves both variables makes part of the slope belong to it, not to spend.

checkpoint.stem: In Leads = 172.5 + 0.0155 × Spend, what does 0.0155 represent?
opts: Leads from a campaign with zero spend
Additional leads per extra dollar of spend, on average
checkpoint.why: The slope is the average change in leads for each extra dollar: about 15.5 per $1,000.

modules.title: Multiple Regression
modules.blurb: Several predictors, each holding the others constant.
concepts: Holding others constant

Multiple regression gives each predictor its own coefficient: the change in the predicted outcome for a one-unit change in that predictor, with every other predictor fixed. Leaving out a driver that moves with an included predictor shifts its effect onto that predictor; that is omitted variable bias.
Dummy variables

Categories become 0/1 columns. A category with k levels needs k − 1 dummies; the left-out level is the baseline. Each dummy coefficient is the difference from the baseline. In NovaTech's model Central is the baseline, so West = 443 means West deals bring about $443 more per month than Central deals, other predictors held constant.
NovaTech's revenue model

Across 1,200 deals: deal size 1.035 (p < 0.001), sales-cycle days 14.65 (p = 0.159), East 171 (p = 0.473), West 443 (p = 0.067); R² = 0.748. Revenue tracks deal size almost dollar for dollar. Adding cycle and region moved R² from 0.7471 to 0.7483, and adjusted R² only to 0.7474, so deal size does nearly all the work.
Overlap: VIF

When predictors move together, coefficients become unstable and standard errors inflate. VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ). Above 5 deserves a look; above 10 is severe. NovaTech's largest VIF is 1.75, and once deal size is in the model the month trend has p = 0.96: the revenue decline runs through shrinking deals.
Yes/no outcomes and honest nulls

Coding readmission as 1/0 gives a linear probability model: each extra chronic condition adds about 0.66 percentage points of risk (p = 0.0001), yet patient-level R² is just 0.001. Significant means real; R² says how much it explains. And a length-of-stay model with R² = 0.0003 should be reported as finding nothing, not used for bed planning.
Specifying before fitting

For Riverside County, choose predictors from policy and theory before seeing results. District-level variables are shared by every applicant in a district, so their effective sample size is the number of districts. Variables like minority share describe the system a group faces, not a trait of the group.
cards: When a missing driver moves with an included predictor, its effect is wrongly credited to that predictor.
A 0/1 column marking a category. k categories need k − 1 dummies.
The category left out of the dummies. Every dummy coefficient is a difference from it.
R² with a penalty for each added predictor. Rises only if a predictor helps more than chance would.
1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ). Measures how much a predictor overlaps with the others. > 5 investigate, > 10 severe.
Regression on a 0/1 outcome. Coefficients are changes in probability; can stray outside 0–1.
Significance says an effect is real. R² says how much of the outcome the model explains. Report both.
Group averages remove individual noise, so unit-level correlations can look far stronger than patient-level reality.

kc.stem: A predictor has four categories. How many dummy variables does the model need?
kc.why: k − 1 = 3. Including all four would duplicate the intercept.

kc.stem: NovaTech's deal-size coefficient is 1.035. Which reading is correct?
opts: Each extra $1 of deal size is associated with about $1.03 more monthly revenue, holding cycle and region constant
kc.why: A coefficient is the change in the outcome for a one-unit change in that predictor, others held constant.

quiz.stem: You add a predictor that has no real relationship with the outcome. What typically happens?
opts: R² falls and adjusted R² rises
R² stays the same or rises slightly; adjusted R² may fall
Both R² and adjusted R² rise sharply
quiz.why: R² never falls when a predictor is added. Adjusted R² penalizes predictors that don't earn their place.

quiz.stem: A predictor has a VIF of 12. What does that indicate?
opts: Severe multicollinearity: its standard error is inflated
quiz.why: Above 10 is severe overlap; coefficients become unstable and look less significant.

quiz.stem: In Mercy Regional's model, P(readmit) = 0.084 + 0.0066 × chronic conditions. An extra chronic condition is associated with:
quiz.why: In a linear probability model, 0.0066 is a change in probability: 0.66 percentage points.

quiz.stem: The chronic-conditions effect has p = 0.0001 but patient-level R² = 0.001. What follows?
opts: The effect is real but explains little of individual variation
quiz.why: Individual readmissions are noisy. The model describes average risk well and individual outcomes poorly.

quiz.stem: Riverside's digital-access % is measured per district and shared by every applicant in it. Its effective sample size is closer to:
quiz.why: A district-level value repeats for every applicant, so it carries only as much information as there are districts.

checkpoint.stem: Sales-cycle days has a coefficient of 14.65 with p = 0.16. What is the right reading?
opts: The data can't distinguish its effect from zero
checkpoint.why: Not significant means the data cannot pin the effect down; it does not prove there is no effect.

modules.title: Checking the Model
modules.blurb: The assumptions that make the numbers trustworthy.
concepts: LINE assumptions

Linearity: average Y changes in a straight-line way with each X. Independence: one error says nothing about another. Normality: residuals are roughly bell-shaped. Equal variance: residual spread is the same at every fitted value. Each has a standard check and a known consequence when it fails.
Residuals vs fitted

Plot each residual against its fitted value. You want a shapeless cloud around zero. A curve signals nonlinearity; a funnel signals unequal variance. NovaTech's plot is centered with no curve, but its spread widens a little at higher values.
Unequal variance and robust errors

NovaTech's Breusch–Pagan test gives p < 0.001: the variance is unequal. Coefficients stay unbiased, but standard errors, p-values and intervals become unreliable. Robust (HC3) standard errors fix this; NovaTech's conclusions all held (deal size p < 0.001; cycle 0.153; West 0.073).
Skew and influence

Length of stay is right-skewed (mean 4.5, median 3, skew 1.97); modeling log(LOS) brings skew to 0.12, and coefficients read as percentage changes. Cook's distance flags influential points; the rule of thumb is D > 4 ÷ n. Verify them, understand the story, refit with and without, report both, and never delete points just to improve fit.
cards: Average Y changes in a straight line with X. Check: residual plot. Failure: wrong shape.
Errors are unrelated. Check: Durbin–Watson (≈ 2 is good). NovaTech: 1.97.
Residuals roughly bell-shaped. Matters most in small samples; large n is protected by the CLT.
Equal residual spread at every fitted value. Its failure is called heteroscedasticity.
Tests whether residual variance changes with the predictors. Small p = unequal variance.
Standard errors that stay valid under unequal variance. In statsmodels: fit(cov_type="HC3").
How much the fitted line changes if one point is removed. Flag D > 4 ÷ n.
Modeling log(Y) tames right skew; coefficients read as approximate % changes.

kc.stem: A residual plot shows residuals positive at both ends and negative in the middle (a U shape). This suggests:
opts: A nonlinear relationship: try a transformation or squared term
kc.why: A curve in the residuals means the straight line has the wrong shape.

kc.stem: With 48 campaigns, the Cook's distance rule of thumb flags values above about:

quiz.stem: Heteroscedasticity mainly affects:
opts: The standard errors, p-values and confidence intervals
quiz.why: Coefficients remain unbiased; inference becomes unreliable.

quiz.stem: A Durbin–Watson statistic of 1.97 suggests:
opts: No evidence that errors are correlated
quiz.why: Values near 2 indicate independent errors.

quiz.stem: An events campaign produced far more leads than predicted and is highly influential. The best first response is:
opts: Delete it so the model fits better
Verify the data, understand why, and report results with and without it
Ignore it because n is small
quiz.why: Influential points are evidence. Check them, explain them, and show their effect.

quiz.stem: Length of stay has mean 4.5 days, median 3 and skewness 1.97. A sensible modeling step is:
opts: Add more predictors until skew disappears
Use the median as the outcome
quiz.why: A log transform pulls in the long tail; coefficients become percentage effects.

quiz.stem: NovaTech's residuals show mild non-normality (Jarque–Bera p = 0.0002) with n = 1,200. This is:
opts: A minor concern, because large samples protect coefficient tests
quiz.why: The central limit theorem makes coefficient tests robust to mild non-normality in large samples.

checkpoint.stem: A residual plot whose spread widens as fitted values grow signals:
checkpoint.why: A funnel is the signature of unequal variance; use robust standard errors or a transformation.

modules.title: Predictive Performance
modules.blurb: Will the model work on data it has never seen?
concepts: Train and test

Fit is measured on the data a model learned from; prediction is measured on data it has never seen. Hold out a random 20% (240 of NovaTech's 1,200 deals), fit on the rest, then score the held-out deals.
Error metrics

R² is the share of variation explained. RMSE is the square root of the average squared error, in the outcome's units, and punishes big misses. MAE is the average absolute miss, the easiest to explain. NovaTech: test MAE $2,705, about 8% of an average deal's $33,745, close to its training MAE of $2,578.
Underfit, overfit, cross-validate

Underfit models are too simple and poor everywhere; overfit models memorize noise and are great on training data but poor on new data. Polynomial curves on the campaigns show it: degree 8 has training error 132 but held-out error 847. K-fold cross-validation rotates the test fold so every case is tested once, giving a stabler estimate.
Regularization and time

Ridge shrinks all coefficients; Lasso can set some exactly to zero, selecting predictors. Offered 34 predictors, Lasso kept 3 with the same test RMSE ($3,397 vs $3,403). For time-ordered data, hold out the most recent period: a trend fit on months 1–18 forecast months 19–24 with a 3.7% average error.
cards: The data the model learns its coefficients from.
Data set aside and never used in fitting; the honest check on prediction.
√[Σ(y − ŷ)² ÷ n]. Typical error in the outcome's units; punishes large misses.
Σ|y − ŷ| ÷ n. The average size of a miss, ignoring direction.
Memorizing training noise: low training error, much higher test error.
Too simple to capture the pattern: poor on training and test data alike.
Split into k folds; each serves once as the test set; average the k errors.
Regularized regression that can shrink coefficients exactly to zero, removing predictors.

kc.stem: A model's errors on four test deals are +$1,000, −$2,000, +$3,000 and −$1,000. What is the MAE?
Your data are 24 months of revenue in time order. The honest way to test a forecast is to:
opts: Hold out a random 20% of months
Hold out the most recent months
kc.why: A random split lets the model peek at the future. Hold out the latest period.

quiz.stem: Model A: training RMSE $2,900, test RMSE $5,800. This pattern indicates:
quiz.why: Error that doubles on new data is the signature of memorizing training noise.

quiz.stem: Compared with MAE, RMSE:
quiz.why: Squaring errors before averaging gives big misses more weight.

quiz.stem: What can Lasso do that Ridge cannot?
opts: Set some coefficients exactly to zero
quiz.why: Lasso's penalty can zero out coefficients, which selects predictors.

quiz.stem: Why use 5-fold cross-validation instead of one split on 48 campaigns?
opts: It removes dependence on which cases happen to land in the test set
quiz.why: Rotating the test fold averages away the luck of a single split.

checkpoint.why: The model is memorizing noise in the training data, which does not repeat in new data.

modules.title: From Output to Decision
concepts: Excel and Python

In Excel, enable the Analysis ToolPak, then Data › Data Analysis › Regression: Y range, adjacent X columns, Labels, 95% confidence, residual plots. In Python, smf.ols("Y ~ X1 + C(Region)", data=df).fit() builds dummies for categories; .summary() gives the full table and .get_prediction() gives forecasts with intervals.
Two kinds of interval

For a $20,000 campaign the point forecast is 482 leads. The 95% confidence interval, 432 to 532, describes the average of many such campaigns. The 95% prediction interval, 142 to 821, describes one campaign. Plan one campaign, month or patient with the prediction interval.
The recommendation chain

Finding → Evidence → Implication → Action → Risk. More spend produces more leads at a rising marginal cost; slope 15.5 per $1,000 (CI 11.9–19.0), elasticity 0.70; the next lead costs about $65 vs $38; cap incremental spend where a lead is worth less than $65 and pilot a reallocation; season and channel may change the picture.
Questions to ask any model
Which decision does it inform? Was it tested on unseen data? How big is the effect in real units? What is missing? Is it association or causation, and what is the plausible range of outcomes?
cards: Excel add-in for regression: Data › Data Analysis › Regression. X columns must be adjacent.
In Excel's ANOVA block, the p-value for the model as a whole.
"Y ~ X1 + X2 + C(Region)": outcome left of ~, predictors right; C() builds dummies.
statsmodels method returning a forecast with its confidence and prediction intervals.
Where the average of many similar cases would fall. Narrow.
Where a single new case is likely to land. Wider, because it includes individual variation.
Size of an effect in real units (dollars, days, patients), not just whether p < 0.05.

kc.stem: You are planning one $20,000 campaign next month. Which range should you plan around?
kc.why: A single case needs the prediction interval, which includes campaign-to-campaign variation.

kc.stem: For multiple regression in Excel's ToolPak, the X columns must be:
kc.why: The Input X Range must be one contiguous block of columns.

quiz.stem: In statsmodels, what does C(Region) in a formula do?
opts: Treats Region as categorical and builds dummy variables
quiz.why: C() marks a column as categorical; statsmodels creates the k − 1 dummies.

quiz.stem: In Excel's regression output, Significance F is:
opts: The p-value for the model as a whole
quiz.why: It tests whether all predictors together explain anything.

quiz.stem: Why is a prediction interval wider than a confidence interval for the same forecast?
opts: It uses a lower confidence level
It includes the individual variation the model cannot explain
It is computed on test data
quiz.why: Averages cancel noise; a single case does not.

quiz.stem: Which statement belongs in the Risk step of the recommendation chain?
opts: Cap spend where a lead is worth less than $65
Budgets may follow the season, and returns may differ by channel
quiz.why: Risk names what could make the conclusion wrong.

quiz.stem: A colleague says “p < 0.05, so the effect is large.” The best correction is:
opts: Agree: small p means large effect
Small p means the effect is distinguishable from zero; size is the coefficient in real units
Small p means R² is high
quiz.why: Significance and size are different questions. Report the effect in dollars, days or patients.

checkpoint.stem: You are planning one $20,000 campaign. Which interval should you plan around?
checkpoint.why: A single case needs the prediction interval, which includes case-to-case variation.

1: Welcome to this lecture on regression and predictive modeling. So far in this course we have described data, reasoned about uncertainty, and tested whether differences are real. Regression brings those ideas together. It lets us measure how an outcome moves with the factors that drive it, and then use that relationship to forecast. Throughout the lecture we will work with real data from three settings: a software company trying to revive growth, a hospital trying to reduce readmissions, and a county agency trying to close an equity gap in benefits processing. Every technique comes with a manager's lens, because the point is not the equation. The point is the decision the equation supports.
4: Here is the roadmap. We begin with foundations: what regression is and the two jobs it does for managers. Then we build simple regression from first principles, one predictor and one line. Next comes multiple regression, where several predictors work together. After that we check the model's assumptions, then evaluate how well it predicts on data it has never seen. We finish by moving from output to decision, in Excel, in Python, and in the language of a recommendation. Each section ends with a short knowledge check.
5: Section one: foundations. Before any equations, we need to be clear about what regression is for, what its vocabulary means, and where it fits in the process of building a model that supports a decision.
12: Section two: simple linear regression. We will build the regression line from first principles, using one predictor and one outcome, so that every number in the output has a clear meaning before we add complexity.
24: Section three: multiple regression. Real outcomes have more than one driver. Multiple regression estimates the effect of each predictor while holding the others constant, and that phrase, holding the others constant, is the most important idea in this section.
37: Section four: checking the model. Every number in a regression output rests on assumptions. In this section we learn what those assumptions are, how to check them with residuals and a few standard tests, and what to do when one fails.
45: Section five: predictive performance. A model can fit the past beautifully and still forecast badly. In this section we learn how to test a model on data it has never seen, how to measure its errors in units managers understand, and how to keep it from memorizing noise.
53: Section six: from output to decision. We finish by running regression in the two tools you will use, Excel and Python, and then by turning output into a recommendation that a leadership team can act on.
62: For further study, the statsmodels documentation covers regression output and diagnostics in depth, and scikit-learn covers train-test splits, cross-validation, and Ridge and Lasso regularization. Kaggle Learn offers short, free, hands-on Python courses. And Microsoft's support pages walk through regression with the Analysis ToolPak in Excel. Work through the regression notebook in Google Colab with the course datasets, and use the diagnostic checklist and the recommendation chain from this lecture in your project.
2: Every manager is already making predictions, usually informally.
A sales director asks how much revenue the next quarter will bring if deal sizes keep shrinking.
A chief quality officer asks which discharged patients are most likely to come back within thirty days.
A public administrator asks how many caseworkers a district needs to bring processing times down.

Each of these is a question about how one quantity responds to others. Regression answers it with an estimate, and just as importantly, with a measure of how far that estimate can be trusted. That second part is what separates an analysis from a hunch.
3: By the end of this lecture you will be able to do five things.
First, explain what predictive modeling is and the role regression plays in data-driven decisions.
Second, build simple and multiple regression models and interpret every coefficient in plain managerial language.
Third, check the assumptions that make those numbers trustworthy, and diagnose problems from the residuals.
Fourth, evaluate how well a model predicts, using R squared, root mean squared error and mean absolute error, and recognize when a model is overfitting or underfitting.
And fifth, run regression in both Excel and Python, and turn the output into a recommendation a leadership team can act on.
6: Predictive modeling uses patterns in historical data to estimate outcomes we have not yet observed, and to decide what to do about them. The workflow has four links.
We start with historical data, for example two years of marketing campaigns, sales deals or hospital discharges.
We fit a model that captures how the outcome moves with its drivers.
We use the model to produce a prediction for a new case, such as next month's campaign, together with a range.
And the prediction informs a decision: how much to spend, how many nurses to schedule, how many caseworkers to hire.
Then the loop closes. The outcome of that decision becomes new data, and the model is checked and refit. A model that is never checked against what actually happened is a model nobody should trust.
7: Regression does two different jobs, and it is worth deciding which one you are doing before you build anything.

The first job is explanation. Here the question is which factors move the outcome, and by how much, holding everything else constant. A hospital wants to know whether weekend discharge raises readmission risk once patient complexity is accounted for. The coefficients are the product.

The second job is prediction. Here the question is what value to expect for a new case. The finance team needs next quarter's revenue figure. Accuracy on new data is the product, and individual coefficients matter less.
The same equation can serve both jobs, but the evidence you need, and the way you judge success, are different. So decide which question you are answering before you build.
8: Every regression has one outcome and one or more predictors.
The outcome, written Y, is the quantity we want to explain or forecast. You will also hear it called the dependent variable or the response.
The predictors, written X, are the factors we believe drive the outcome. They are also called independent variables or, in machine learning, features.
Here is how this maps onto our three settings. For NovaTech, the outcome is monthly revenue from a deal, driven by deal size, sales-cycle length and region.
For Mercy Regional, the outcome is whether a patient is readmitted within thirty days, with predictors such as chronic conditions, length of stay, follow-up and weekend discharge.

For Riverside County, it is the number of days an application takes to process, driven by caseworker ratio, digital access, language barriers and program type. Notice that an outcome can be a dollar amount, a count of days, or even a yes-or-no event.
9: Regression is one of the most widely used tools in management analytics, and it appears in every sector.

In business, firms forecast sales from historical revenue, marketing spend and seasonality, and estimate customer lifetime value from tenure and behavior. In healthcare, hospitals predict readmission risk or recovery time from clinical history to target follow-up care.

Hospitals also forecast patient census to set nurse staffing. In public administration, agencies model service processing times to set staffing levels, and evaluate whether programs reach the people they are meant to serve. The common thread is a measurable outcome, a set of plausible drivers, and a decision that depends on the relationship between them.
10: A good regression follows a disciplined process of six steps.
First, frame the decision. What will change depending on the answer, and what outcome measures it?
Second, gather and clean the data: fix types, handle missing values, and make sure categories are coded consistently.
Third, explore. Plot the outcome against each predictor and look for direction, shape and unusual points before fitting anything.
Fourth, fit the model, estimating the coefficients by least squares.
Fifth, evaluate it: check the assumptions and test it on data it has not seen.
Sixth, communicate and act, translating coefficients into dollars, days or patients, with an honest range of uncertainty.
Fitting takes seconds in software. Most of the value, and most of the mistakes, happen in framing, exploring and evaluating.
11: Knowledge check. A hospital asks whether weekend discharges raise readmission risk once patient complexity is accounted for. Which job is regression doing? Option A: predicting the exact readmission risk of one specific patient. Option B: explaining a driver's effect while holding other factors constant. Option C: summarizing readmission rates by day of the week. Option D: ranking departments from best to worst.
The answer is B, explaining a driver's effect while holding other factors constant.

The phrase "once patient complexity is accounted for" is the signal. The hospital wants the weekend coefficient from a model that also contains measures of complexity, such as chronic conditions and length of stay. It is not trying to forecast one patient's risk, and a simple table of rates by day of the week would not hold complexity constant.
13: Every regression should start with a picture.

This scatter plot shows all forty-eight NovaTech marketing campaigns. Each dot is one campaign, with spend on the horizontal axis and leads generated on the vertical axis. We read a scatter plot for four things.
Direction: the cloud rises, so campaigns that spent more tended to generate more leads.
Form: the pattern is roughly linear, although it seems to flatten at the highest spend levels.
Strength: the points cluster reasonably tightly, and the correlation is about 0.79.

And unusual points: one campaign near twenty-six thousand dollars generated more than thirteen hundred leads, far above its neighbors. Keep that point in mind. It will come back when we discuss influence.
14: Simple linear regression summarizes the cloud with a straight line.
The model says Y equals b-zero plus b-one times X, plus an error term, epsilon.
The intercept, b-zero, is the predicted value of Y when X is zero. It is where the line meets the vertical axis.

The slope, b-one, is the change in the predicted Y for each one-unit increase in X: the rise for a run of one. It is the number managers care about most, because it answers the question, if this driver moves, how much does the outcome move?
The error term captures everything the line does not: other drivers, measurement noise, and plain randomness. It is the vertical gap between a point and the line.
Once we estimate the line from data, we write Y-hat for the predicted value, and the gap between the actual and predicted value is called the residual.
15: Many lines could be drawn through a cloud of points, so we need a rule for choosing one.

For any line, each point has a residual: the vertical distance between the actual value and the line's prediction. Some residuals are positive and some are negative, so simply adding them would let misses cancel out.
Instead we square each residual. The squares show it: every miss now counts, and a miss twice as large counts four times as much.

Ordinary least squares, or OLS, chooses the intercept and slope that make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. That single rule produces a unique line, and it is the line every statistics package reports by default.
16: Least squares has a closed-form solution, and it is worth computing once by hand so the output never feels like a black box.

The slope equals the sum of the cross-products of deviations from the means, divided by the sum of squared deviations of X. The intercept equals the mean of Y minus the slope times the mean of X, which guarantees the line passes through the point of means.

For the forty-eight campaigns, mean spend is about sixteen thousand four hundred fifty-eight dollars and mean leads is 426.9. The sum of cross-products is about 139 million, and the sum of squared spend deviations is about 8.99 billion.
Dividing gives a slope of 0.01546 leads per dollar.
The intercept is 426.9 minus 0.01546 times 16,458, which is 172.5 leads.
So the fitted line is leads equals 172.5 plus 0.01546 times spend, or about 15.5 leads for every thousand dollars of spend.
17: Here is the campaign data again.
Now the fitted line is laid over the data. The model reads: leads equal 172.5 plus 0.0155 times spend.

Interpreting the slope is the heart of the exercise. Campaigns that spent one thousand dollars more generated, on average, about 15.5 more leads. Notice the wording: on average, and associated with. This is a summary of what happened across these campaigns, not a guarantee for any single one.

The intercept says a campaign with zero spend would generate about 172 leads, but no campaign in the data spent less than about twenty-eight hundred dollars. The intercept anchors the line. It is not a forecast for doing nothing, and reading it as one is a classic extrapolation error.
18: Here is the manager's lens on that slope: turn the coefficient into a price.
If one dollar buys 0.01546 leads, then one additional lead costs about one divided by 0.01546, or roughly sixty-five dollars.

Compare that with the average cost per lead across the campaigns, about thirty-eight dollars. The next lead is far more expensive than the typical lead, which is exactly what happens when the cheapest audiences have already been reached.
The model also gives a planning number: a twenty-thousand-dollar campaign is expected to produce about 482 leads.

The decision question is whether an extra lead is worth more than about sixty-five dollars to NovaTech. If the expected value of a lead, after conversion, is lower than that, more spend will produce more leads and still lose money.
19: R squared answers a simple question: how much of the variation in the outcome does the model account for?
Least squares splits the total variation into two parts: the total sum of squares equals the regression sum of squares plus the error sum of squares.
Start with the total sum of squares, the spread of leads around their mean. For our campaigns it is about 3.43 million.
The regression sum of squares is the part the line explains: 2.15 million.
The error sum of squares is the part left in the residuals: 1.28 million.
R squared is the explained share: 2.15 divided by 3.43, or 0.627. Spend accounts for about sixty-three percent of the campaign-to-campaign variation in leads.

In simple regression, R squared is also the square of the correlation: 0.79 squared is about 0.63. R squared describes fit. It says nothing about cause, and what counts as a good value depends on the field.
20: A slope estimated from forty-eight campaigns would be a bit different with another forty-eight. Three numbers describe how much to trust it.
The standard error measures that sampling wobble: 0.00176 leads per dollar.
Dividing the slope by its standard error gives the t statistic, 8.79. The slope sits almost nine standard errors away from zero.
The matching p-value is far below 0.0001, so a slope this large would be extraordinarily unlikely if spend truly had no relationship with leads.
For a manager, the confidence interval is the most useful of these numbers.
We are ninety-five percent confident the true slope lies between 0.0119 and 0.0190, that is, between about twelve and nineteen leads per thousand dollars, around a point estimate of 15.5.

Zero, which would mean no relationship, is far outside that range. Even the pessimistic end of the interval is well above zero, and planning with the range is more honest than planning with a single number.
21: Look again at the top end of the scatter plot. The biggest campaigns sit below the straight line, a sign that each additional dollar buys fewer leads as spend grows.

One way to capture that curvature is to take logarithms of both variables and fit a straight line on the log scale. The result is: log of leads equals minus 0.69 plus 0.70 times log of spend. On the original scale, that line becomes the curve.

In a log-log model the slope is an elasticity. A ten percent increase in spend is associated with about a 6.9 percent increase in leads, not ten percent. That is diminishing returns expressed as a single number.
The curved model also fits a little better, with R squared of 0.69 against 0.63. A straight line is a starting point, not a commitment. Always ask whether the relationship bends.
22: A regression slope measures association. Whether it measures cause depends on how the data were generated.
Consider the marketing data: spend and leads, linked by the slope we estimated.

But budgets are not assigned at random. They are often largest in peak season or during a product launch, when buyers are already in the market. Season then drives both spend and leads, and part of the slope reflects the season, not the spend.

The same trap appears in every track. In healthcare, the sickest patients often receive the most follow-up calls and still readmit more, so a naive regression can make follow-up look harmful. In public administration, districts with the largest backlogs are often the ones that receive extra caseworkers, so staffing can look useless.
Three habits protect you: name the plausible confounders and include them, think about which way causation could run, and where the stakes are high, test with a pilot or a phased rollout.
23: Knowledge check. The fitted slope is 0.0155 leads per dollar of spend. Which statement is correct? Option A: spending one thousand dollars more will cause exactly 15.5 more leads. Option B: campaigns that spent one thousand dollars more generated about 15.5 more leads, on average. Option C: a campaign with zero spend will generate about 172 leads. Option D: because R squared is 0.63, the slope is 63 percent accurate.
The answer is B: campaigns that spent a thousand dollars more generated about 15.5 more leads, on average.

Option A overstates it twice, with the word cause and the word exactly. Option C treats the intercept as a forecast, but no campaign spent anywhere near zero. Option D confuses two different ideas. R squared tells us how much variation the model explains overall. The precision of the slope is described by its standard error and confidence interval.
25: Most outcomes have several drivers. NovaTech's revenue depends on deal size, but perhaps also on how long deals take to close and which region they come from.
Multiple regression extends the equation to include all of them: Y-hat equals b-zero plus b-one X-one plus b-two X-two, and so on up to b-k X-k.
With deal size as the only predictor, its slope absorbs anything else that happens to move with deal size.
With several predictors in the model, deal size, sales-cycle days and region each get their own coefficient.

Each coefficient now has a precise meaning: the change in the predicted outcome for a one-unit change in that predictor, holding every other predictor in the model constant. If we leave out a driver that is related to both the outcome and an included predictor, the included predictor absorbs its effect. That distortion is called omitted variable bias, and adding the right predictors is the main defense against it.
26: Regression needs numbers, so categories such as region are converted into dummy variables: columns that equal one when a condition is true and zero otherwise.

NovaTech has three regions: Central, East and West. We pick one as the baseline, here Central, and create a dummy for each of the others. A West deal has West equal to one and East equal to zero. An East deal has East equal to one. A Central deal has both equal to zero.
The rule is: a category with k levels needs k minus one dummies. Including all three would duplicate the intercept and break the model.

Each dummy coefficient is the difference from the baseline. If the East coefficient were 171, East deals would bring in 171 dollars more per month than Central deals, holding the other predictors constant.
Yes-or-no variables, like weekend discharge in healthcare, are simply a single dummy: yes equals one, no equals zero.
27: Now a full multiple regression on real data. We use all 1,200 NovaTech deals and predict each deal's monthly revenue from its deal size, its sales-cycle length in days, and its region, with Central as the baseline.
The table shows what statsmodels reports for each term: the coefficient, its standard error, the t statistic, the p-value and the ninety-five percent confidence interval.

Deal size has a coefficient of 1.035 with a standard error under 0.02, and a p-value that rounds to zero. Sales-cycle days has a positive coefficient of 14.65, but its p-value is 0.159. The East and West dummies are 171 and 443, with p-values of 0.473 and 0.067.

For the model as a whole, R squared is 0.748 and adjusted R squared is 0.747, the overall F statistic is 888, and the residual standard error is about 3,347 dollars. Now let us read each line the way a manager would.
28: Here is how to translate each line of that table.

Deal size: each additional dollar of deal size is associated with about one dollar and three cents of monthly revenue, holding cycle length and region constant, and the effect is unmistakably significant.

Sales-cycle days: each extra day is associated with about fifteen dollars more revenue, but the p-value of 0.16 and a confidence interval running from minus six to plus thirty-five dollars mean we cannot distinguish the effect from zero.
Region: compared with Central, East deals bring about 171 dollars more and West deals about 443 dollars more per month, but neither difference is significant at the five percent level.
Finally, the intercept has no stand-alone meaning, because a deal of zero dollars is not a deal. It simply anchors the model.
Remember: not significant does not mean no effect. It means these data cannot pin the effect down.
29: R squared never falls when you add a predictor, even a useless one, because least squares can always use an extra column to shave a little off the residuals.

Adjusted R squared corrects for that. It applies a penalty based on the number of predictors, k, relative to the number of observations, n, and it rises only if a new predictor improves the fit by more than chance would.
Compare two NovaTech models. With deal size alone, R squared is 0.7471.
Adding sales-cycle days and the two region dummies lifts R squared to 0.7483.
And adjusted R squared rises to only 0.7474. The bars are nearly identical: three extra predictors bought about one tenth of one percent of explained variation.

Deal size is doing almost all the work. Because R squared never falls, never use it alone to choose between models. A simpler model that explains nearly as much is easier to explain, easier to maintain, and often predicts just as well.
30: When predictors move together, regression struggles to separate their effects. Coefficients become unstable, standard errors inflate, and a genuinely important predictor can look insignificant. This is multicollinearity.
The variance inflation factor, or VIF, measures it. For each predictor, regress it on all the other predictors and take one divided by one minus that R squared.
A VIF of one means no overlap. Above five deserves investigation, and above ten is severe, a signal to drop or combine predictors.

In the NovaTech data, deal size has been shrinking while sales cycles have been lengthening over time, so we test a model that adds the month number. The VIFs are 1.30 for deal size, 1.45 for cycle days and 1.75 for month, all comfortably below five.
And something revealing happens: once deal size is in the model, month has a p-value of 0.96. Revenue's decline over time runs through shrinking deals. Time itself adds nothing.
31: Through the manager's lens, the NovaTech model points clearly to where the revenue problem lives. A model points to where to look; it does not say why.
Deal size is the lever. Revenue tracks it almost dollar for dollar, so every thousand dollars lost per deal costs roughly a thousand and thirty-five dollars a month.
Once deal size is known, the passage of time adds nothing, which tells leadership the slowdown is a deal-size story rather than a calendar story.
And regional differences are small and statistically indistinguishable, so reorganizing territories is unlikely to be the fix.

The decision question is what is shrinking the deals: discounting, a shift toward smaller customers, product mix, or longer negotiations. Regression narrows the search; the next analysis has to answer why.
32: Now healthcare, where many outcomes are yes or no. Was the patient readmitted within thirty days? Code readmission as one for yes and zero for no, and ordinary regression still works. This is called the linear probability model, and each coefficient is a change in probability.

Using all 12,400 Mercy Regional discharges, we regress readmission on the number of chronic conditions. The bars show observed readmission rates by condition count, from about eight percent with no chronic conditions to seventeen percent with eight. The line is the fitted model.
The fitted model says the probability of readmission equals 0.084 plus 0.0066 times the number of chronic conditions.

Each additional chronic condition is associated with about two-thirds of a percentage point higher readmission risk. The p-value is 0.0001, and the confidence interval runs from about 0.3 to 1.0 percentage points.
One caution: a linear probability model can predict values below zero or above one at the extremes. Logistic regression, the standard tool for yes-or-no outcomes, is built to avoid that.
33: Here is a result that surprises many students. The chronic-conditions effect is highly significant, yet the model explains almost nothing about individual patients.
At the patient level, across 12,400 individual yes-or-no outcomes, R squared is just 0.001.

Now group the patients by condition count and regress the nine group readmission rates instead. R squared jumps to 0.78. Nothing about the relationship changed. Averaging simply removed the individual noise.

Here is why. An individual readmission is close to a coin flip with a slightly weighted coin. Knowing a patient has five conditions rather than two shifts the odds a little, but it cannot tell you who will actually return.
This is also why correlations computed on unit-level or department-level averages often look far stronger than the patient-level reality.
For a manager, the model is useful for allocating follow-up resources across groups, and weak for flagging one specific patient.
So keep the two ideas apart. Significance says the effect is real. R squared says how much of the outcome it explains. Report both.
34: Not every model finds something, and reporting that honestly is part of the job. Suppose Mercy Regional wants to predict length of stay for bed planning, using age, chronic conditions, ICU admission and number of procedures.
The overall F test, which asks whether all the predictors together explain anything, has a p-value of 0.51.
And none of the four predictors is significant at five percent. The closest, number of procedures, has a p-value of 0.075.

The correct conclusion is clear: these variables do not explain length of stay in this data. The responsible next step is to look for better predictors, such as primary diagnosis, discharge barriers or social support at home.
The irresponsible step would be to build a bed-capacity plan on a model with an R squared near zero simply because it produced coefficients.
35: Now public administration, using the Riverside County benefits case, where SNAP, TANF and Medicaid applications take anywhere from eleven to thirty-four days to process, depending on the district. Before running anything, an analyst specifies the model.

The outcome is processing days per application. Candidate predictors include the caseworker ratio, the district's digital-access rate, whether the applicant faced a language barrier, the program type coded as dummies, and office hours.

The coefficients are then read with the same template as before. For example: holding staffing and program constant, each ten-point increase in digital access is associated with b fewer processing days.

Two cautions are specific to this setting. First, district-level predictors are shared by every applicant in a district, so the effective sample size for them is the number of districts, eight, not the thirty-four thousand applications.
Second, variables such as minority share or income describe the system a group faces, not a trait of the group. Interpret them as gaps in service, and report them with care.
Why specify the model first? Choosing predictors from theory and policy, before seeing results, protects against fishing for significance.
36: Knowledge check. In the NovaTech model, the West coefficient is 443 with a p-value of 0.067, and Central is the baseline. What is the correct reading? Option A: West deals earn 443 dollars more per month than East deals. Option B: West deals earn about 443 dollars more per month than Central deals, holding deal size and cycle constant, but the gap is not significant at five percent. Option C: West is the strongest region and should receive more sales reps. Option D: the coefficient is wrong because its p-value is above 0.05.

A dummy coefficient compares its category with the baseline, not with another dummy, so A compares the wrong regions. The comparison holds deal size and cycle length constant, and with a p-value above 0.05 we cannot rule out a true difference of zero. C turns a non-significant estimate into a staffing decision, and D confuses not significant with wrong. The estimate is the best guess the data can give; it is simply imprecise.
38: Ordinary least squares rests on four assumptions, easy to remember with the word LINE.
L is linearity: the average outcome changes in a straight-line way with each predictor. You check it with a residuals-versus-fitted plot, and if it fails, the coefficients describe the wrong shape.

I is independence: one observation's error tells you nothing about another's. It is checked with the Durbin-Watson statistic or by thinking about how the data were collected, and it fails with repeated measures over time or clustered groups, producing standard errors that are too small.
N is normality of residuals, checked with a histogram, a Q-Q plot or the Jarque-Bera test. It matters most for small samples.

And E is equal variance, also called homoscedasticity: the spread of residuals is the same at every level of the prediction. It is checked with the Breusch-Pagan test, and when it fails the coefficients are still fine but the p-values and confidence intervals are not.
39: The residuals-versus-fitted plot is the single most useful diagnostic.
Each point is one deal: its predicted revenue on the horizontal axis and its residual, actual minus predicted, on the vertical axis. A sample of 250 NovaTech deals is shown.
What we want is a shapeless cloud centered on zero.
Two shapes are warning signs. A curve, with residuals positive at both ends and negative in the middle, means the relationship is not linear, and the model needs a transformation or a squared term.
A funnel, where the spread widens as the prediction grows, means unequal variance.
Our plot is centered on zero with no curve, which supports linearity. The spread does widen slightly at higher predicted values, which is worth testing formally, and we will do that next.
40: The Breusch-Pagan test formally asks whether the residual variance changes with the predictors.
For the NovaTech model the p-value is below 0.001, so we reject equal variance. The model is heteroscedastic.
What does that break, and what does it not? The coefficients themselves are still unbiased. What becomes unreliable are the standard errors, and therefore the p-values and confidence intervals.
The standard remedy is heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors. In statsmodels you add one argument when fitting: cov type equals H C 3.
Here are the results side by side. Deal size remains significant, with a p-value below 0.001. Sales-cycle days moves from 0.159 to 0.153, East from 0.473 to 0.469, and West from 0.067 to 0.073.
Every conclusion holds. That is the outcome you hope for, and checking is how you earn the right to say so.
41: Some outcomes are heavily skewed, and length of stay is a textbook case.
Most Mercy Regional patients stay one to three days, but a long tail stays two or three weeks.
The mean is 4.5 days while the median is 3, and the skewness is about 2. Skewed outcomes often produce skewed residuals and unequal variance.
The standard fix is to model the logarithm of the outcome. Taking the log of length of stay pulls in the long tail and brings the skewness down to about 0.1.

Coefficients in a log-outcome model are read as approximate percentage changes. A coefficient of 0.05 means about five percent longer stays per unit of the predictor. That is often a more natural way to talk about stays, costs and processing times, where effects tend to be proportional rather than fixed.
42: An outlier is an observation far from the pattern. An influential observation is one that, if removed, would noticeably change the fitted line. Cook's distance measures that influence for each observation.

A common rule of thumb flags values above four divided by n, which for forty-eight campaigns is about 0.083. Three campaigns exceed it. Campaign C-043, a digital paid campaign spending about fifty-one thousand dollars, produced 658 leads, below what its spend predicts, with a Cook's distance of 0.37. Campaign C-037, another large digital campaign, sits at 0.18.

And campaign C-046, an events campaign spending about twenty-six thousand dollars, produced 1,336 leads, far above prediction, with a distance of 0.34. It is the unusual point from our first scatter plot. Did it over-deliver for a reason that can be repeated?
What should a manager do? First, verify the data. Is it an entry error, or a real result?
Second, understand the story. Was it a one-off, or a repeatable success?
Third, refit the model with and without these points, and report both versions.
What you should never do is delete points simply because the model fits better without them. That is hiding evidence.
43: Here is the full diagnostic toolkit applied to the NovaTech revenue model, one row per check.

Linearity, from the residual plot: no curve, so it passes. Independence, from the Durbin-Watson statistic, where values near two are good: 1.97, so it passes. Normality, from the Jarque-Bera test: p equals 0.0002, a detectable but mild departure. With 1,200 observations, the central limit theorem protects the coefficient tests, so this is a minor concern. Equal variance, from Breusch-Pagan: p below 0.001, so it fails, and we have already applied robust standard errors with no change in conclusions. Multicollinearity, from the VIFs: the largest is 1.75, well below five, so it passes.
A table like this belongs in any serious regression report. It shows the reader what was checked, what failed, and what was done about it.
44: Knowledge check. A residual plot shows a funnel, with residuals spreading out as fitted values grow. What is the best response? Option A: delete the observations with the largest residuals. Option B: keep the coefficients, but use robust standard errors or model a log outcome. Option C: add predictors until the funnel disappears. Option D: ignore it, because R squared is high.

A funnel is the signature of unequal variance. The coefficients remain unbiased, but the standard errors, p-values and intervals cannot be trusted, so we use robust standard errors or model the logarithm of the outcome. Deleting the largest residuals hides evidence. Adding predictors at random invites overfitting. And a high R squared tells us nothing about whether this assumption holds.
46: R squared measures how well a model fits the data it was built from. But a forecast is used on new cases, so the honest question is how the model performs on data it has never seen. The simplest test is a train-test split.
Set aside a random twenty percent, 240 deals, as the test set, and do not touch them. The remaining 960 deals form the training set.
Fit the model on the training deals only. Every coefficient comes from training data.
Then use that fitted model to predict the 240 test deals, and compare the predictions with the actual outcomes.

If performance on the test set is close to performance on the training set, the model has learned something general. If it drops sharply, the model has memorized patterns that were specific to the training data.
47: Three metrics summarize predictive accuracy, and each is shown here for the training deals and the unseen test deals.
R squared, which we know, is the share of variation explained. For the NovaTech model it is 0.752 on training and 0.729 on test.

Root mean squared error, or RMSE, is the square root of the average squared prediction error. It is in the outcome's own units, dollars here, and because errors are squared it punishes large misses heavily. It is 3,322 dollars on training and 3,417 on test.

Mean absolute error, or MAE, is the average size of the miss, ignoring direction. It is the easiest to explain: on a typical deal, the forecast is off by this many dollars. It is 2,578 on training and 2,705 on test.

So on a typical unseen deal, the forecast misses by about 2,700 dollars, roughly eight percent of the average deal's monthly revenue of 33,745 dollars. The small gap between training and test says this model generalizes well.
48: A model can fail in two opposite ways: it can be too simple, or too flexible.

This chart makes the difference visible on the marketing campaigns. We fit polynomial curves of increasing complexity, from a straight line, degree one, up to degree eight, and measure two errors: on the training data, and with cross-validation on held-out data. Training error falls steadily, from 160 leads to 132, because a more flexible curve can always bend closer to the points it has seen. But held-out error tells the real story. It stays near 167 for the simple models, then climbs steeply.
An underfit model is too simple to capture the real pattern, and it performs poorly on training and test data alike.
A good fit captures the pattern, with similar error on training and test data.
An overfit model is so flexible that it memorizes the noise in its training data. It performs well on training data and badly on new data.
At degree eight, training error is 132 while held-out error is 847. The extra wiggles fit noise, and noise does not repeat.
49: A single train-test split depends on which observations happen to land in the test set, and with small datasets like the forty-eight campaigns, that luck matters. K-fold cross-validation removes it. Split the data into k equal folds, five here.
In round one, fit the model on four folds and test on the first.
In round two, the second fold becomes the test set.
Round four tests on the fourth fold.
And round five on the fifth. Every observation is used for testing once and for training four times.
Average the five test errors. The result is a more stable estimate of how the model will perform on new data. The held-out errors on the previous chart were five-fold cross-validated.
In Python, scikit-learn's cross val score function does all of this in one line.
50: When there are many candidate predictors, which ones belong in the model? Regularization answers that automatically by adding a penalty for large coefficients.
Ridge regression shrinks all coefficients toward zero, which stabilizes models with correlated predictors.
Lasso regression shrinks them too, but it can push some coefficients exactly to zero, removing those predictors entirely. That makes Lasso a feature-selection tool.

Here is an experiment on NovaTech. We offered the model thirty-four candidate predictors: deal size, cycle days, month, two region dummies, and twenty-nine dummies identifying the sales rep, with the penalty chosen by five-fold cross-validation.
Lasso keeps just three: deal size, the West dummy, and one rep.
On the test set, ordinary regression with all thirty-four variables has an RMSE of 3,403 dollars, and the three-variable Lasso model 3,397.
Same accuracy, eleven times simpler. A simpler model is easier to explain, cheaper to maintain, and less likely to break.
51: When data are ordered in time, a random split is not an honest test, because it lets the model peek at the future. Instead, hold out the most recent period.

Here we take NovaTech's average monthly revenue per deal, fit a straight-line trend on months one through eighteen, and forecast months nineteen through twenty-four, which the model has never seen. The dashed lines show the ninety-five percent prediction band.
The fitted trend is revenue equals 38,357 dollars minus 352 dollars per month, with an R squared of 0.87 on the training months.

Over the six held-out months, the forecast misses by 1,067 dollars on average, a mean absolute percentage error of 3.7 percent. Five of the six actual values fall inside the band; month twenty dipped below it, a reminder that a band is not a guarantee.

Two cautions. A trend model assumes the past pattern continues; it would miss a turnaround. And it explains nothing. We already know from the multiple regression that the decline runs through deal size.
52: Knowledge check. Model A has a training error of 2,900 dollars and a test error of 5,800. Model B has a training error of 3,300 dollars and a test error of 3,400. Which should NovaTech use for forecasting? Option A: Model A, because it has the lowest training error. Option B: Model B, because its error on unseen data is lower and close to its training error. Option C: either one, because both were fit to the same data. Option D: neither, because both have errors above zero.

Test error is the evidence about how a model will perform on cases it has not seen, which is exactly what a forecast is. Model A's error doubles on new data, the signature of overfitting. Its low training error is a measure of memorization, not skill. Model B performs almost as well on unseen deals as on the data it learned from, and that consistency is what makes a forecast trustworthy.
54: In Excel, regression lives in the Analysis ToolPak, in five steps.
Enable it once, through File, Options, Add-ins, then Manage Excel Add-ins, and tick Analysis ToolPak.
Then go to Data, Data Analysis, and choose Regression.
Set the Input Y Range to the outcome column, leads generated, and the Input X Range to the predictor columns, spend here. For multiple regression, the X columns must sit next to each other.
Tick Labels if you included headers, set the confidence level to ninety-five percent, and tick Residuals and Residual Plots.
Send the output to a new worksheet.

Here is the output for the marketing model. The regression statistics block gives R squared, 0.627, adjusted R squared, 0.619, and the standard error, 166.8 leads. The ANOVA block gives the F statistic and Significance F, the p-value for the whole model. And the coefficients table gives the intercept, slope, standard errors, p-values and confidence limits.
They are the same numbers we derived by hand.

56: Every forecast should come with a range, and there are two different ranges to choose from.
Take a twenty-thousand-dollar campaign. The point forecast is 482 leads.
The ninety-five percent confidence interval, 432 to 532 leads, describes where the average of many such campaigns would fall. It is narrow because averaging cancels out noise.

The ninety-five percent prediction interval, 142 to 821 leads, describes where a single campaign is likely to land. It is much wider because it includes the campaign-to-campaign variation the model cannot explain.

Use the confidence interval when you are reasoning about averages, such as a full year of campaigns. Use the prediction interval when you are planning one campaign, one month, or one patient. Quoting the narrow interval for a single case is one of the most common, and most costly, overstatements in practice.
57: Regression output is not a recommendation. A recommendation has five parts, and here they are for the marketing model.
Finding: what the analysis shows, in one plain sentence. More spend produces more leads, at a rising cost per additional lead.
Evidence: the numbers that support it, with their uncertainty. A slope of 15.5 leads per thousand dollars, with a confidence interval of 11.9 to 19, and an elasticity of 0.70.
Implication: what it means in money, time or service terms. The next lead costs about sixty-five dollars, compared with an average of thirty-eight.
Action: what to do, specifically, and ideally in a way that can be tested. Cap incremental spend where a lead is worth less than sixty-five dollars, and test a reallocation with a controlled pilot.
Risk: what could make the conclusion wrong. Budgets may follow the season, and returns may differ by channel.
Finding, evidence, implication, action, risk. That chain turns output into a decision.
58: Here is a manager's checklist for any regression that lands on your desk, whether an analyst built it or a vendor is selling it.
First, which decision does it inform? If nothing changes depending on the answer, the model is decoration.
Second, was it tested on data it did not see? Training fit is not forecasting skill.
Third, how big is the effect in real units, dollars, days or patients, rather than just a p-value?
Fourth, what is missing? An omitted driver can distort every coefficient in the model.
And finally, the two questions that decide how much weight the model deserves: is this association or causation, and what is the plausible range of outcomes rather than the single point estimate?

60: Before you move on, here are six misconceptions to retire.
First, a high R squared proves causation. It does not. R squared measures fit, and causation depends on how the data were generated.
Second, a p-value below 0.05 means the effect is large. It means the effect is distinguishable from zero. Size is measured by the coefficient, in real units.
Third, not significant means no effect. It means the data cannot pin the effect down.
Fourth, more variables always make a better model. Adjusted R squared and test error often say otherwise.
Fifth, the intercept always has a meaning. Often it lies far outside the observed data.
And sixth, a model that fits the past will predict the future. Only out-of-sample testing can show that, and even then, conditions can change.
61: To close, five ideas to carry forward.
Regression measures how an outcome moves with its drivers, and each coefficient is an effect holding the others constant: an association, unless the design supports cause.
Every estimate comes with uncertainty. Plan with confidence intervals for averages and prediction intervals for single cases, not with single numbers.
Check the assumptions, look at the residuals, and say what you did when something failed.
Judge a predictive model on data it has never seen, and prefer the simpler model when accuracy is equal.
And translate output into decisions: finding, evidence, implication, action, risk. A regression earns its place when it changes what a manager does.
